Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images US supreme court US supreme court allows Trump to keep building $400m White House ballroom Justices’ 5-4 ruling permits Trump administration appeal to block lower court order halting above-ground work Chris Stein in Washington Mon 31 Aug 2026 18.13 EDT First published on Mon 31 Aug 2026 16.40 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A divided US supreme court has permitted Donald Trump to continue building his controversial $400m White House ballroom despite legal challenges, raising the likelihood it will be completed. In a 5-4 ruling, the justices permitted the Trump administration’s request to ⁠block a lower court order which had halted above-ground construction of the project while a lawsuit by a historic preservation group seeks to block it. The US president, who demolished the historic East Wing of the White House last year to make way for planned ballroom, has repeatedly touted it as “a gift” to the US people. Renderings show most detailed vision for Trump’s White House ballroom Read more Monday’s decision from the supreme court comes after the court’s conservative chief justice, John Roberts, issued a temporary order that had enabled work to continue. However, Roberts joined the court’s three liberal justices in dissenting from the majority’s decision and wrote that the construction was “likely unlawful”. The court’s decision may allow Trump to bring to fruition a project that is at the center of his ambition to remake the US capital in his image. Since taking office, he hass ordered the National Mall’s reflecting pool covered in blue liner, proposed a $250m renovation to the Kennedy Center performing arts center that would see his name emblazoned on its side, and is pursuing plans to renovate a golf course and build a massive arch . While some projects have hit legal roadblocks, such as when a judge ordered Trump’s name removed from the Kennedy Center, or descended into farce, like when the reflecting pool line began falling off, the supreme court’s decision today is a victory for the president. Trump celebrated Monday’s ruling in a post on Truth Social, boasting that the White House complex would be “one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington DC”, with construction to be completed by the summer of 2028. In an unsigned opinion, the five conservative justices said the National Trust for Historic Preservation in the United States lacked standing to bring a lawsuit against the project. The trust had centered its argument on the declaration of a board member, the architectural historian Alison Hoagland, who said the ballroom was an “aesthetic, cultural and historical” affront because of its design, and that she would suffer “injuries” when viewing it in Washington DC . “The government is likely to prevail in showing that the Trust lacks standing to challenge the East Wing project,” the majority opinion read. “This court has not found standing in circumstances like these before. To the contrary, we have repeatedly held that mere offense, disagreement, or distaste does not qualify as a concrete and particularized injury.” The justices also agreed that the government would suffer “irreparable harm” if construction is stopped, or only allowed to continue on a military installation set to be built underneath the ballroom while the above-ground portion remains unfinished. The majority ultimately side stepped the question of whether the president’s decision to tear down a chunk of a building that rotates between presidential officeholders was actually legal. “Today, we do not pass upon the legality of the government’s East Wing project,” they wrote. The dissenting justices – Roberts, together with Democratic-appointed justices Elena Kagan, Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson – argued that the project is unlawful because Congress has not approved it. In his opinion, Roberts wrote that the construction is a “likely infringement of the legislature’s power of the purse and authority to regulate federal property in the District of Columbia to continue,” and says the majority’s ruling “is no victory for the separation of powers”. “The ballroom is a building or structure being erected on federal park grounds – President’s Park – in the District of Columbia. Yet Congress has not passed any law resembling ‘express authority’ for the executive’s construction of it,” the chief writes. He also disagreed that the potential injuries to Hoagland are insufficient for the historic trust to sue, saying she was “deeply committed to the preservation of such historic American buildings” through her work with the association. “Hoagland’s injury suffices for standing,” Roberts wrote, likening the impact of the White House’s transformation on her to how “an environmentalist can sustain a concrete, particularized aesthetic injury from the extinction of a particular animal or the transformation of a particular forest or river that he regularly enjoys”. Miliband says intelligence sharing from the UK has not aided the Israeli occupation or its actions in Gaza and the West Bank. Photograph: Hazem Bader/AFP via Getty Images View image in fullscreen A man watches Israeli bulldozers demolish a Palestinian home in Hebron, in the occupied West Bank. Miliband says intelligence sharing from the UK has not aided the Israeli occupation or its actions in Gaza and the West Bank. Photograph: Hazem Bader/AFP via Getty Images Foreign policy Israel sanctions will not hurt intelligence sharing between spy agencies, says Miliband UK foreign secretary says international community including US shares ‘frustration’ at Israel’s failure to constrain illegal settlers Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Wed 9 Sep 2026 12.14 EDT Last modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 15.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google British intelligence has been given assurances by its Israeli counterpart that information sharing with the UK will continue as before, Ed Miliband , the foreign secretary, has said. The disclosure counters predictions that his decision to impose a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements would lead to a collapse in cooperation between the agencies. The exchanges of information are seen as mutually beneficial and it is understood that Israeli intelligence was never willing to become mired in any political dispute between the two governments. Miliband insists the intelligence sharing from the UK has not aided the Israeli occupation or its actions in Gaza and the West Bank . Miliband also expressed confidence that the US shared some of his exasperation with Israel’s reluctance to constrain the settlers in the West Bank, or to engage fully with the 20-point plan for Gaza set out by Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. As yet there has been no explicit criticism of the UK’s actions by the White House. Trump avoided taking a hard stance when pressed about the coalition of countries, including the UK, France, and Canada, that have imposed new sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank. “I’ll be speaking to Israel, I’ll be speaking to them, and I’ll find out what’s their thinking,” he said on Wednesday. Trump, now locked in fighting midterm elections, appears reluctant to leap to the aid of Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, who persuaded him to go to war against Iran. That decision has pushed oil prices beyond $100 a barrel, helping to swell a threatened “blue wave” that could leave the Democrats in charge of both the House and the Senate. There is also cross-party concern in the US at the violent tactics adopted by some Israeli settlers. Ed Miliband gives statement on UK plans to sanction Israel – watch live Miliband said on Sky News on Wednesday: “We obviously talked to the Americans in advance of our announcement. I think the whole international community, let me say this, has been quite frustrated, to put it mildly, with some of the actions of the Israeli government. “I think there is real concern about what is happening … underlying so much of the conflicts in the Middle East is this failure to really grasp the situation between Israel and Palestine . “It’s in our interest to act not just because it’s standing up for our values, but because it’s in our interests to have this two-state solution as a rock of stability in the Middle East.” The US decision not to oppose the UK over its sanctions and ban on trade with the Israeli settlements follows conversations between Trump and the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, on Monday, as well as previous diplomatic exchanges at lower levels. Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, was careful not to endorse the UK sanctions, but affirmed he shared the objective of securing greater stability. Miliband can also claim credit for persuading Canada and France to join the trade ban , the surprise element in the package announced on Tuesday. The agreement came together late in the process. Eight other European countries have announced their intention to introduce such measures or to support the measures within the EU, a statement of solidarity that represents probably less of a shift than headlines might suggest. Some of the signatory countries had already taken steps independent of the EU, or had long been advocating for measures such as suspension of the Israel-EU trade agreement. Map For France, the decision to join the British initiative was formalised relatively late during Emmanuel Macron’s trip to London, when he met Burnham on 3 September and celebrated the display of the Bayeux tapestry at the British Museum. France acted after a Franco-Swedish proposal made to the EU27 in April appeared to be making little progress. The French plan aimed to establish an embargo or tariff on products from the occupied territories, but resistance from a constellation of countries including Germany, Italy and Bulgaria blocked progress. The commission also appeared to raise objections. Paris last year had led the push to recognise the state of Palestine as critical to the two-state solution, but much of the French diplomatic energy had subsequently drifted. The UK, along with Jordan, will hold a meeting concerning improving humanitarian supplies into Gaza at the UN general assembly later this month. In advance of Miliband’s statement, Trump had been hinting that he might support the Argentinian claim to sovereignty over the Falklands, a proposal mooted by Netanyahu’s son. But in a little-noticed move likely to please Washington, Miliband this week supplemented the action against Israel by announcing fresh nuclear-related sanctions against Iran, including targeting Iranian ships involved in “malign behaviour”. The UK also said it was backing a motion to be put to the UN stating Iran was in breach of its obligations on nuclear proliferation. The new sanctions are extended to cover energy, software, metals, gold and related activities such as shipping, insurance and banking. Most Iranian aircraft will be prohibited from landing in the UK. In response to the UK ban on goods, not due to come into force for at least six months, Israel has said it will: close the British consulate in in occupied East Jerusalem ; remove British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat in southern Israel; terminate the UK’s role in training Palestinian Authority forces in the West Bank; and deny 12 mainly leftwing MPs entry to Israel. http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27930.text: Big News Network.com Imazsia Chinese Film Week 2026 opens in Budapest BUDAPEST, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- The Imazsia Chinese Film Week 2026 opened Friday evening in the Hungarian capital Budapest, with the Chinese film "Dear You" making its Hungarian premiere as the opening film. At the opening ceremony, Chinese Ambassador to Hungary Gong Tao said that since its launch, the Imazsia Chinese Film Week has continued to bring outstanding Chinese films to Hungarian audiences and played a positive role in promoting film and television exchanges between the two countries. Gong expressed hope that the two sides would carry out more practical cooperation in film screenings, creative exchanges and talent training, and continuously enrich the content and forms of China-Hungary people-to-people and cultural exchanges. Also speaking at the opening ceremony, Levente Horvath, president of the Hungarian-Chinese Youth Friendship Association, said that more and more high-quality works are emerging from China's film industry. These films have distinctive Chinese characteristics while telling human stories with universal significance. Gabor Cserkesz, vice president of the Hungarian-Chinese Friendship Association, said the deep and enduring partnership between China and Hungary rests not only on economic cooperation, but should also be strengthened through bridges of ideas and culture. He said the Imazsia Chinese Film Week provides audiences with a valuable opportunity to see, approach and understand China through Chinese cinema. According to Viktoria Varadi, founder of the Imazsia Chinese Film Week, this year's event is supported by the China Film Administration, the Chinese Embassy in Hungary and the China Film Archive, among others. From Sept. 11 to 18, Chinese films including "Dear You," "Journey to the West" and "A Mongolian Tale" will be screened in Budapest and Szeged, she added. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Kyiv and Kharkiv have experienced rolling blackouts and water outages this week. Photograph: Gleb Garanich/Reuters View image in fullscreen Kyiv and Kharkiv have experienced rolling blackouts and water outages this week. Photograph: Gleb Garanich/Reuters Ukraine Analysis Power plant attacks increasingly reflect Russian blueprint to make Ukrainian cities unliveable Andrew Roth in Kyiv Kremlin turning to punishment of Ukraine’s population in major cities as frontlines remain frozen Europe live – latest updates Fri 16 Oct 2026 11.28 EDT Last modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 11.57 EDT Share As Russian missiles and drones have systematically slammed into power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv this week, the rolling blackouts and water outages have increasingly resembled a supposed Russian blueprint to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities seen by the Guardian. Even as Donald Trump unilaterally declared an “energy ceasefire” last week between Moscow and Kyiv, Russia continued with its methodical and devastating strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, in particular in Kyiv, in a strategy meant to punish Ukraine’s population and drive the country to capitulation. Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses Read more The potential goals of the Russian campaign, according to an assessment seen by the Guardian that Ukrainian intelligence said it intercepted from Russia last month, range from “degrading the quality of life” of Ukrainians through power outages to fully shutting off the water supply, which the document cooly predicts would cause the “deterioration of sanitary conditions and the forced outflow of residents from cities.” The document does not specify which Russian agency developed the assessment, which is titled Analysis of Ukraine’s Energy, Housing and Utilities Sectors, includes vulnerable Ukrainian energy grid targets and even contemplates strikes against high-risk sites, including the switchyards at several nuclear power plants. But several European officials familiar with the document have said it is likely to have been produced by analytical departments linked to the Russian military or intelligence agencies, and that copies have circulated in Ukraine in previous years. This year, however, Russia appears to be putting those plans into practice. On Tuesday night, Russian strikes hit three major power plants in the Kyiv region – Combined Heat and Power Plants 4 and 5, and the Trypillya Thermal Power Plant in the Kyiv region – as well as a major electrical substation that transfers electricity from two of the country’s main nuclear power plants to the capital. Those, along with other substations that make up the “Kyiv energy ring” that helps bring electricity from across the country to the capital, have all been targets of a Russian barrage that, if it succeeds, could threaten a humanitarian catastrophe in a city of 3 million people. Ukraine’s energy minister first briefed European allies last month about the plan, a copy of which was first reported on by the New York Times. Russia has stepped up its attacks on the Ukrainian power grid precisely as Washington and Kyiv are embroiled in a major political quarrel. The Guardian is withholding some specifics of the military assessment at the request of Ukraine’s energy ministry, which said it could aid in further strikes against the country. “There are two large documents, written very coldly and very clearly, with tables showing the number of weapons needed for each facility to destroy it,” Ukrainian energy minister Denys Shmyhal said last month. “The types of weapons range from ballistic missiles to jet-powered and conventional drones. We understand how they are going to act.” The leaked documents identify bottlenecks and prescribe the number of ballistic and hypersonic cruise missiles and jet-powered drones needed to knock out power plants and substations with brutal efficiency. If that was done, it could destroy more than 90% of the power that Kyiv is budgeted for each winter, the document predicts, plunging the city into the dark and cold. A worst-case scenario could lead to blackouts lasting up to 20 hours a day until damaged equipment is repaired, according to expert projections. The strikes on Ukraine’s energy system have become the country’s new frontlines – and the country is badly outgunned, as its stocks of US-provided PAC-3 missiles have dwindled. Zelenskyy this week castigated city authorities for poor planning for the winter and for failing to protect the city’s energy infrastructure. Protests over heat and electricity blackouts are also planned for Saturday, highlighting how the difficult conditions in winter could provoke a political crisis for the wartime government. Economic Pravda, a leading Ukrainian news site that covers business, reported on Thursday that the three major power plants in Kyiv no longer have the ability to generate electricity, leaving the city more reliant on electricity brought from elsewhere in the country (the government generally does not confirm specific damage to critical infrastructure). The outlets’ experts predicted that, given a moderate winter and quick repairs of damaged substations, Kyiv residents could face up to eight hours of blackouts a day. Its worst case scenario of frigid temperatures and frequent attacks would leave Kyiv in the dark for up to 20 hours a day. This is no accident for the Kremlin, which has increasingly turned to punishing Ukraine’s population in major cities as the frontlines of the conflict have frozen. “Last year, we were really on the brink,” said Volodymyr Fesenko, a Ukrainian political analyst. “But the risk this year will be even worse, so the plan [to attack Ukrainian infrastructure] does seem realistic. There’s a very high chance that Russia tries to break us this winter.” If the Kremlin believed in the chance of a clean military victory before now, he added, it may now believe that not to be possible, and focus on destroying Ukraine’s remaining infrastructure rather than trying to capture it. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion The secret plan, which officials here say was intercepted by Ukrainian intelligence and then briefed to senior European diplomats by Shmyhal last month, sets itself several goals: to destroy electricity generation, heating, water and sewage systems in such a way as to to make life in Ukrainian cities unliveable. Destroying electrical generation alone, it says, would lead to a “significant decrease in the quality of life of the population.” To do so, it specifies the number of weapons that should be allocated – Geran 4/5 jet-powered drones and hypersonic or cruise missiles – in order to destroy key infrastructure such as thermal power plants, substations, water pumping stations and more. Considering strikes against the basis of Ukraine’s water, sewage and heating systems, the document says it would create a “large-scale municipal infrastructure crisis.” When contacted by the Guardian, the Ukrainian Energy Ministry said that the document contained information that could aid in attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. It did not reply to questions on how the current Russian bombing strategy matched with the proposals made in the document, or which Russian agency had developed the plans.
